intro: This page asks you only what you alone can decide ([[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]). Each question says what it decides, what it means in practice at a show, for the GM at a failure, for the designer and for a production that adopts the engine, and the options with what each means and what each costs. Where the agent running the pass has a sound view, it gives a recommendation. Where the answer is a values call of yours, it says in one line what we need from you. Answer in the chat by a question's letter or its title. Each question stands alone: answer any of them, in any order, and leave the rest for later.

Every question here but the last passes four tests. Only you can answer it: it is about what the product must do or allow, for whom, or which of two goods matters more, never about how to build it. The decision record does not already answer it. At least one of the six decisions ahead on [[page:design]] depends on it. And it is needed before the panel's blind round. The last question, on the panel, is yours for another reason: adding to what the blind round gets changes a decision you made, and only you can change it. Two of version 9's eighteen questions are still yours, reworded below; the rest are now the readings of your words to confirm, the agent's calls to overrule and the requirements to review, under their own headings below, and the [[page:changes]] says where each of the eighteen went.

You also asked to see the specific conflicts between the qualities, and what each means in practice, before saying which win. The first group is those conflicts. Its introduction names the ones the requirements already answer, some resting on your decisions and some on targets still marked proposed or partly settled, and which way. Its questions answer the ones still open.
Below the questions: what comes in the design rounds, in order; the later choices kept for those rounds; and everything decided, by topic, from the decision record.

groups.title: Where the qualities pull against each other
intro: The quality targets on [[page:requirements]] fall under twelve qualities. In the top-level design some of them pull against each other. The requirements already answer most of those conflicts: some rest on your decisions, some on targets still marked proposed or partly settled, which you can flag in the review below; the panel designs to them as they stand:
The designer's iteration speed against the promise “[[promise:J5]]”. A change reaches a game only between games, or the engine refuses and says why ([[qt:QT9]], [[ex:EX2]]).

The designer's iteration speed against safe release and rollback. Packs publish at any time and the engine changes only between events ([[qt:QT42]]); a pack that needs an ability this engine lacks is refused at publish with the ability named ([[qt:QT10]]); abilities are only ever added ([[qt:QT21]]).

Standalone and offline against easy to understand and change. A standalone tablet is a second decider in the code, but there is one decider per game ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]). Whether the engine and the tablet run one body of rules or two kept equal by tests is a later choice for the design rounds.
Privacy and access against staying up through a live show. Passes survive a reconnect, a restart and a machine swap, and nobody logs in again mid-show ([[qt:QT31]], [[qt:QT3]], [[qt:QT42]]).

Privacy and access against the promise that the night can be told afterwards. Game data stays on the kit; you move the record, and the director's console stays a separate program outside the engine ([[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]], [[qt:QT30]]).
Operating without technical help against privacy and access. The kit holds its own passes, the GM logs in once a night, and staff who log in hold the game's controls ([[qt:QT14]], [[qt:QT31]]).

Running well at the size of a show against more than one copy, kit or pack. A few dozen devices is the setting the panel gets ([[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]), and phones are measured before the first is admitted ([[qt:QT34]]).
Testable without the live show against easy to extend. Every added program or device kind comes with a software stand-in and its tests ([[ex:EX15]], [[qt:QT26]]).
Every screen telling the truth against standalone and offline. A standalone game says standalone, and every service the engine runs reads not installed tonight, grey ([[qt:QT37]]).

Seven conflicts stay open, and six questions below answer them: two conflicts meet in “The show machine fails mid-game”; one, easy to extend against easy to understand and change, gives two questions, “What a game's maker may build inside the pack” and “How an extension for all games reaches a production”; and one, the standing rule that phones and hardware scanners stay equal in ability, against standalone and offline, sits with the standalone games below. Each question names the qualities, says what happens at a show under each answer, and names the decision ahead that waits on it.

questions.title: A GM tablet cut off from the engine
questions.decides: Staying up through a live show against every screen telling the truth. What a GM tablet does with a scan while it cannot reach the engine for a short time, a dropped wifi or an engine restart. What the GM may tell the team at that moment. What happens when the connection returns and the engine disagrees with what the tablet showed. The same answer holds for the first minutes of a longer failure, before the GMs know whether the show machine is coming back.
evidence: Your decision settles that the game goes on ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]), and the quality target [[qt:QT7]] proposes that a refused scan never reads as complete; you settled that only for a standalone game, and the networked part is proposed. Open: what the tablet shows meanwhile, and who wins a conflict.

At a show. The tablet's wifi drops for a minute. A team hands the GM a token. Today the tablet shows “Transaction Complete” with points, from its own copy of the rules, and keeps the scan to send to the engine later ([[flaw:C9]]). If another tablet sold the same token during that minute, the engine refuses the kept scan on reconnect, and the GM has already told the team it earned money. The quality target [[qt:QT3]] asks that the game carries on and that the GM can always see what became of such a scan, and leaves what the tablet does with it meanwhile, and who wins a conflict, to this question.

For the GM at the failure. With a refusal the GM says “give me a minute, the connection is down” and the line waits. With a kept scan the GM says “it is in, your result shows when we are back”. With a provisional verdict the GM says “you earned fifty thousand” and may have to take it back. Your words are that pausing a game for a lost connection is the worst scenario, and that the GMs need to know their fallbacks. The question is what the fallback shows.
For the designer. Nothing changes in the pack. A designer of a game with group bonuses should know that a provisional bonus can be undone.

For a production adopting the engine. A venue with worse wifi than yours makes this the common case. A production with one GM tablet can never have a conflict, so for them a kept scan and a provisional verdict come to the same thing. A production with four tablets at four tables has conflicts every time the wifi drops.

Under the two options that keep the scan, you also set the conflict rule: when two tablets both sold one token during the gap, who wins. The earlier by the tablets' clocks (clocks differ). The first to reach the engine (luck). Or the GM decides from a red row and tells the losing team. This is a choice between fairness by time and simplicity.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included” names this question in what it decides. Refusal means the engine is the only decider and tablets are screens. Keep-and-label means the protocol has a provisional state and the engine orders scans by their time. Provisional verdicts mean the rules run in two places and a reconciliation exists. “The published protocol's form” follows: what every reply carries (how sure the engine is) depends on whether provisional replies exist. “How the engine holds the game's state” follows too, since kept scans must be ordered against the engine's record.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on the agent's question about a GM tablet losing the show machine. [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]], whose first reading (a tablet keeps taking scans) is listed under the readings to confirm below. [[qt:QT3]], [[qt:QT7]], [[flaw:C9]], and the finding of the two clocks under [[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]. The record holds no conflict rule.

options.label: Refuse while cut off.
options.means: The GM sees a plain reason and nothing is kept; teams wait. The engine is the only decider, the tablet holds no game fact of its own, and the protocol needs no “not yet decided” state.
options.cost: Every wifi drop costs show time, which is close to the pause you called the worst scenario.

options.label: Keep and label.
options.means: The tablet records the scan as kept and not yet decided, shows no points, and shows the GM a list of kept scans. On reconnect the engine decides each in order and the tablet shows the final answer; a kept scan refused later becomes a red row the GM must act on. GMs learn one habit: “in, pending”.
options.cost: The protocol carries a provisional state in replies and in the tablet's list, and the engine must order kept scans by when they happened, which meets the finding of the two clocks.

options.label: Keep and decide provisionally under the shared rules.
options.means: The tablet applies the same rules the engine would, from its last known copy of the game, and shows the verdict and the points marked provisional. The engine confirms or overturns on reconnect. The richest fallback for the GM.
options.cost: The game's rules must run equally on the engine and the tablet; every fact the tablet shows must carry “provisional” in the protocol; a conflict rule and a conflict screen exist. The most to keep equal across two places, for years.

questions.recommendation: Keep and label. It keeps the game going, as you decided, and it keeps the tablet from telling a team something the engine has not decided, which [[qt:QT7]] proposes for a networked game and your words on fallbacks support. It costs a provisional state in the protocol and one habit for the GMs. What we need from you beyond that is the conflict rule: when two tablets both sold one token while apart, the earlier by the tablets' clocks, the first to reach the engine, or the GM decides from a red row. That is a choice between fairness by time and simplicity, and the design cannot make it for you.

questions.title: The show machine fails mid-game
questions.decides: Staying up through a live show against standalone and offline, and against every screen telling the truth on the public screens. What a networked game does when the show machine stops and does not come back for the rest of the night. What fallbacks the GMs must have in front of them at that moment. What the players may lose, and what they must never lose. How the results come back together afterwards. Whether a game may change from networked to standalone while running, and what that does to [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]].
evidence: Settled: no game mixes networked and standalone devices, and the game must go on ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]], [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]). Settled for the players' own devices: a scanner shows the player that a scan is kept and not yet sent, and never promises a video it cannot start ([[qt:QT40]]). Open: how the game goes on, and what the audience's screens do.

At a show. Fifty minutes in, the show machine's power supply dies. The TV freezes on the scoreboard. The music stops. The players' phones and the hardware scanners stop sending; the hardware scanner keeps each scan on its card, shows a red Disconnected, and for a video token says rescan later, which cannot work; the phones say offline. The GM tablets lose the engine. Today each tablet has its own copy of the game as of the last message and keeps scanning with its own verdict. Nothing merges two tablets' records afterwards, and no spare takes over.

For the GM at the failure. Your words: the GMs need to know their available fallbacks. The tablet should show them as a red row with actions, the pattern [[qt:QT15]] settles. Which actions exist is this question. “Carry on from this tablet.” “Switch to the spare.” “End the game from here.” Each is a different engine.

For the designer. Cues stop with the machine. The designer must know which effects die with it: video, music, lights, the TV, the game clock. That is the same list a standalone game gives up (the question “What a standalone game gives up, and what it keeps”).

For a production adopting the engine. A production with no spare machine. A production whose show is mostly the TV, for whom carrying on means little. A production that runs two games a night and cannot afford a lost one. Each would choose differently; the engine must say which fallbacks it offers.

For the players. You asked for as little effect on the player experience as possible. The design cannot promise the TV and the videos without a second machine. You must say what the players may lose for the rest of a night (video, music, the public evidence screen) and what they must never lose (their scans counted exactly once, no team paid twice for one token). On the public screens there is a second choice: when the engine goes silent, [[qt:QT5]] asks the TV to stop its clock and show it as unconfirmed, which is honest and visible; the alternative is a TV that keeps counting by itself, which is smooth and may be wrong.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “How the engine holds the game's state”, the first and hardest to reverse. A spare that takes over live needs a record that can be copied as it changes; carrying on from tablets needs tablets that hold enough of the record to finish a game; a single store on one machine serves neither. “Where authority lives across devices” follows: whether a tablet or a spare may become the decider, and when. “How one engine runs as many separate copies” follows: a standby is a copy of the engine with the show's identity. “The published protocol's form” follows: how a device finds the engine again under a new machine, and whether a pass issued by one machine holds on another.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on the agent's question about a GM tablet losing the show machine. [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]], whose second reading says the design must say how a networked game carries on if the show machine itself fails, and names its meeting with [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]] as a question for you. [[qt:QT1]] (the machine comes back: settled; this question is when it does not), [[qt:QT5]], [[qt:QT15]], [[qt:QT38]], [[qt:QT40]], [[qt:QT42]], [[flaw:N1]].

options.label: Carry on from the tablets and reconcile afterwards.
options.means: Each GM tablet keeps taking scans, as kept or as provisional under the question above. The GMs end the game from the tablets; the night's record is assembled from their records with the conflict rule. The player devices keep their scans and reach the record only when a machine comes back, or through a collection step after the show. The players lose video, music and the TV for the rest of the night.
options.cost: Every tablet must hold enough of the game to finish it (the teams, the claims, the scores, the pack it ran), and a merge exists for several tablets. The cheapest kit, and a recovery the GMs must rehearse.

options.label: A spare machine takes over at once.
options.means: A second show machine, or a tablet running an engine of its own, holds a live copy of the game's record, takes the engine's name on the kit's own network when the first falls silent, and every device finds it again, the way [[qt:QT42]] already asks devices to carry on when the old machine is replugged. The players lose a minute.
options.cost: The engine's record must be copied live as it changes (a numbered log of facts), the kit's name must move between machines, and passes must hold on both. The most to build and to own (a second machine in every kit), and the strongest promise.

options.label: A cold spare from the last saved record.
options.means: A second machine or a tablet starts the engine from the latest saved copy of the game, kept every few seconds on the tablets or on a stick. The GM starts it by hand; the tablets re-send what they kept since the copy.
options.cost: Between the two above in cost and in the players' loss.

options.label: Declare the game standalone once, for the rest of the night.
options.means: One GM tablet becomes the decider from its last copy of the game; the other devices join it (which needs a channel between devices, in effect a small engine on the tablet) or stop. This would amend [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]: a game's declaration could change once, one way, for the whole game, with every device told. It keeps “never mixed”, since after the change no device is on an engine.
options.cost: An amendment to your decision, which only you can make; a small engine on the tablet.

options.label: Pause until the machine returns.
options.means: Listed only to say it is out. Your words call it the worst possible scenario.
options.cost: The show stops.

questions.recommendation: From you, in one line: which of the first four fallbacks the engine must offer (one or more); whether the TV may keep counting while the engine is silent (yes or no); and whether a game may be re-declared standalone once (yes or no), which amends your decision on standalone games only if you say yes. What the players may lose follows from the fallback you pick; add to it only if you want more protected than their scans counted once.

questions.title: Release day: what must update together, and how long older devices work
questions.decides: Safe release and rollback against easy to extend and operating without technical help. Whether a new version of the engine requires every device and pack to be at the matching version (everything updates together), or the engine must keep working with older GM tablets, phones, hardware scanners and packs for a stated time. How long that time is. Whether a mismatch refuses the device or warns the GM. Whom the promise is for: your kit, or every adopter's.
evidence: You said yes, generally, to everything updating together, and asked what the question means in practice and how it affects the design and the build, especially in the long term once the new engine runs ALN. The explanation follows. Settled already: the show machine keeps one written list of what it should carry and names any piece that differs ([[qt:QT41]]); replugging the old machine undoes a release ([[qt:QT42]]). Open: what happens to the piece that differs, and for how long an older piece works.

What the two phrases mean. “Everything updates together” means one release moves the engine, the GM tablet's app, the phones' page, the hardware scanners' firmware and the protocol between them, and the engine refuses anything at another version. “Older versions keep working with a newer engine” means the engine accepts a device or a pack from an earlier release for a stated time, and the protocol is built so that it can.

Today, the GM tablet's app. The engine serves it, so a tablet that reloads after the engine is updated gets the new app. But a tablet that was open before the update, or one holding the app in its browser's cache, keeps running the old app against the new engine until it reloads. At connection the tablet sends its app version and the fingerprint of the pack it loaded; the engine records the version, uses it only to label the station in its list, and writes a pack mismatch to its log only ([[flaw:C12]]). The list of messages the tablet listens for is kept by hand in the tablet's code; a message the engine adds and the tablet does not know never arrives, with no error ([[flaw:C14]]).

Today, the phones' page and the hardware scanners. In a networked game the engine serves the phones' page too, from a copy placed in its public folder; the page caches itself under a name that must be changed by hand to make phones refresh. The hardware scanners' firmware changes only by cable; the board leaves no room for an update over the air. Their token list, pictures and sounds sync at boot from the engine. So a hardware scanner is the device most likely to be older than the engine, and a change to the token file it reads breaks every scanner that was not flashed.

Today, packs and the protocol. Packs are published separately, at any time. The engine refuses a pack whose format version does not match exactly, a pack that requires an ability the engine lacks, and a pack that names a minimum engine version the engine does not meet; the GM tablet applies only the exact format check. The protocol is two written lists (web requests and live messages), the pack's formats and the venue profile's format, checked by a few tests, and every program copies the names by hand. So today nothing enforces “together” and nothing promises “older works”. Mixtures happen silently: a rollback can leave the machine running pieces from two releases ([[flaw:C15]]), and a tablet at the wrong version is a log line.

In the long term, for your kit. Once the new engine runs ALN, your kit updates between events ([[qt:QT42]]): build the new machine, check it against one written list of what it should carry ([[qt:QT41]]), rehearse, swap by replugging ([[ex:EX17]]). The pieces that can still lag behind the engine on a show night are the hardware scanners (cable), tablets that did not reload, the standalone phone page's own copy of the pack (which changes only when the page is republished), and packs published later than the engine. The published protocol is what makes each of these either refused or tolerated.

In the long term, for adopters. Other productions have their own release pace, their own fleets of cable-updated devices, and perhaps add-ons or their own builds (the question “How an extension for all games reaches a production”). They build against the protocol and the pack format ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]). For them, a protocol that may change shape at every release with no window is a reason not to adopt, or to copy and freeze. A protocol with a window is a promise you must keep for years.

At a show, under each answer. A hardware scanner missed its cable update and connects to the new engine. Under everything-together the engine refuses it, the GM's tablet names it, and the scanner is useless tonight unless someone has a cable and a laptop. Under a window it works tonight and the GM's tablet shows “older firmware, update before the next show”. Packs already have their rule and it does not change here: a pack that needs an ability this engine lacks is refused at publish with the ability named ([[qt:QT10]]), and abilities are only ever added ([[qt:QT21]]), so an old pack runs on a new engine.

How the answer changes the protocol and the build. Under everything-together the protocol has one version number for the whole release; messages may change shape freely between releases, since no two versions ever meet; code on every side is generated from one definition per release; the test bench tests one combination; and the hardware scanners must be at the release before the show, which means either a cable step on the pre-show checklist at every release or a firmware update over the kit's network at boot, which the design rounds would have to add and which has its own cost (room on the scanner for two copies of its program, a fallback that cannot leave the board unable to start). Under a window every message carries its version; inside the window changes are additive (fields are added, never removed or renamed, and a device ignores what it does not know); the engine accepts the current version and a stated number of earlier ones and tells the GM which devices are behind; the test bench runs the engine against each supported device version, a set of combinations that grows with the window; and a written rule says when a version is dropped.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “The published protocol's form” says in what it decides that it settles the version rules; the item above is what each answer does to them. “How today's engine moves to the new design” follows in part: the swap from the show machine in use now to the new show machine is itself a release, and whether old devices may meet the new engine during the move depends on this.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on release day. [[qt:QT41]], [[qt:QT42]], [[ex:EX17]], [[qt:QT10]], [[qt:QT21]]. Today's code: when a tablet connects, the engine records its version and only logs a pack mismatch; the GM tablet's list of messages is kept by hand; the hardware scanner's firmware updates only by cable.

options.label: Everything updates together.
options.means: One version for the release; the engine refuses any device at another version; the tablet and phone apps come from the engine, so they move with it; hardware scanners must be flashed before the show; packs are checked at publish as now.
options.cost: The simplest protocol and one combination to test, and show-night work at every release for every cable-updated device, for you and for every adopter.

options.label: Together for what the engine serves, a window for the rest.
options.means: The engine forces a stale tablet or phone app to reload, so nothing it serves is ever at another version. Cable-updated devices and packs work for a stated window (one or two engine versions back), and the GM's tablet shows which devices are behind.
options.cost: The hardware scanner's part of the protocol is kept small and changed rarely, with additive changes only inside the window; tests of the engine against each supported scanner version; a rule for when a version is dropped. Cable visits when you choose, not every release.

options.label: A window for everything.
options.means: Every message carries its version; the engine speaks to older tablets, phones, scanners and packs within the window.
options.cost: A version on every message, the engine and each device agreeing on a version when they connect, more combinations to test and a written rule for when an old version stops working, kept forever. The most freedom for adopters.

questions.recommendation: Together for what the engine serves, a window for the rest. Your lean is everything together (“Generally speaking, yes”). The agent recommends one exception, for cable-updated devices, as its own view: anyone with a fleet of hardware scanners needs it, and the scanner asks for little (a token list, one scan, a batch of scans, the engine's health, its assets), so keeping its part of the protocol small and stable is cheap. From you: how long the window is (one or two engine versions back), and whether a device outside it is refused or only warned about.

questions.title: What a game's maker may build inside the pack
questions.decides: Easy to extend against easy to understand and change, and the standing rule of parity between phones and hardware scanners against standalone and offline. How far a game's own maker may go inside the pack, with no developer. Values in tables, as today: modes by their flags, scoring tables, groups, cues on a clock. Rules the designer writes as “when this happens, do that”, wiring triggers the engine knows to responses the engine knows; your example is players changing the room's lighting by scanning tokens on a player scanner. Or scripts, code the designer writes into the pack. And whether such rules must also run where there is no engine, on a standalone tablet or on a hardware scanner alone, since phones and hardware scanners stay equal in ability and designers change pack data, never device code.
evidence: Settled: no word of ALN's inside the engine ([[qt:QT20]]); designers change pack data, never device code; a whole game is built without code ([[qt:QT12]]); parity is in ability, not in screens; hardware scanner work waits on no game. Your decision keeps the two kinds of extension apart and leans, in tentative words, to the game's own maker building the first kind inside the game ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]). Open: how far the pack goes, and whether pack rules must run on a scanner alone.

For the designer. The requirements already put your lighting example in tables: the settled case [[ex:EX22]], due with players' phones, lets the pack say what a scan causes, and [[ex:EX25]] has the designer write “this token's scan triggers that look” there, with no developer. What tables cannot do is a combination no declaration yet names, such as a scan of a token in this group lighting this role only while the clock is in this phase; each such combination waits for a developer to add a declaration for it. Today a game played only on GM tablets reaches video through one standing cue per token, which is the tables-only workaround until that declaration exists ([[ex:EX22]]). With when-then rules the designer writes any such combination in the design tool and plays it within minutes, which is the loop the standing rules call the point of the engine work. With scripts the designer can do anything, and the check at the desk can promise little.

At a show. A rule the designer wrote misfires: every scan flips the lights. The GM must be able to switch that rule off from the tablet, as a standing cue is switched off today, and the check at publish must have refused rules that cannot run (a lighting role the venue profile never bound). A rule that runs on the engine is one more thing the GM's Show Control section lists.

For the people maintaining the engine. Tables keep the engine small and readable. A rule format is a second language to version, check, test on two games and document for adopters, and it grows unless someone says no. Scripts need a fenced-off place to run, with limits, and a way to keep a script from harming the show or the kit.

For a production adopting the engine. A theatre company with no developer wants to combine abilities themselves. A company with a developer may prefer code and find a rule format limiting. The hardware scanner matters here: a rule “when scanned, play this sound” must run on the device alone in a standalone game, so the scanner's firmware must carry a runner for whatever rules the pack may hold, or the scanner asks the engine and a standalone scanner runs only what a device alone can.
Your words add one more thing for later: rules a game's maker builds might be shared with other game makers. That is a build consequence (the format must be exportable), not a question now.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “How games and venues extend the engine”: what a pack may declare is in what it decides, and the difference between tables and rules is the difference between a configured engine and an interpreting one. “The published protocol's form”: the pack is one of the protocol's files, and a rule format is the largest thing it could carry. “Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included”: a rule runner on the tablet and on a hardware scanner alone is a second place rules are decided.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on extensions, which the record keeps in your tentative wording. [[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]], which leaves open which piece each kind of extension changes. The standing rules “Designers change pack data, never device code”, “Phones and hardware scanners stay equal in ability” and “Games are playtested without code or settings files”. [[qt:QT12]], [[qt:QT21]], [[ex:EX3]], [[ex:EX10]], [[ex:EX22]], [[ex:EX25]].

options.label: Tables of values only.
options.means: Every new combination is an ability a developer adds, named in the pack's list of required abilities. The engine stays as today in kind; the hardware scanner's firmware stays simple.
options.cost: The designer's loop closes at every combination no declaration yet names, and a developer's additions carry all growth beyond the declared ones.

options.label: Declared when-then rules over the engine's abilities.
options.means: The pack names triggers the engine knows (a scan of this kind, a clock mark, a phase change, a cue finishing) and responses the engine knows (play, light, score, show, hold), and the designer wires them. Most new mechanics need no developer; the rule format is what adopters learn.
options.cost: A rule format inside the pack and so inside the published protocol; a check at publish that refuses rules the engine or the venue cannot run; a runner in the engine and, for standalone games, on the tablet; a listing on the GM's tablet; the hardware scanner either asks the engine (networked) or runs the subset a device alone can (standalone). It must be kept small or it becomes a programming language by accident.

options.label: Scripts in the pack.
options.means: The designer writes code into the pack and can do anything.
options.cost: A fenced-off place to run with limits, a versioned scripting language; the hardware scanner cannot run it; hard to check at the desk; the standing rule that games are built without code is gone.

questions.recommendation: Declared when-then rules over the engine's abilities, kept small. Your lighting example fits in tables once the pack says what a scan causes, so this question is about the combinations after it. Rules are the only option that keeps the designer's loop open for those (built by the game's maker, played within minutes, with no developer), which your tentative words lean to, without giving up the check at the desk or the standing rule that games are built without code. In a networked game the hardware scanner asks the engine; in a standalone game it runs only the subset a device alone can, and the pack says which rules those are. From you: whether that standalone subset is enough, or whether a rule that cannot run on a scanner alone should keep a game from being declared standalone.

questions.title: How an extension for all games reaches a production
questions.decides: Easy to extend against easy to understand and change, and against safe release and rollback. When a developer gives the engine a response it could not give before, your example being audio in several rooms through a program such as Snapcast, how that reaches a production. Only through the engine's main release. Also as an add-on a production installs beside its engine, at places the engine leaves for additions. Or as a production's own changed build of the engine, with no promise from the engine. And what the engine promises about add-ons it did not ship: whether it lists them in its version, tests against them, or refuses ones it does not know.
evidence: Settled: an ability the engine lacks is added once for every game, and the games already running do not change ([[qt:QT21]]); the pack lists the abilities it requires, and the check at publish refuses a pack that needs one this engine lacks ([[qt:QT10]]). Your decision names this question as open, in your words “how those extensions then interact with the main release of the engine” ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]).

At a show. A production runs the main release and an add-on for multi-room audio. The add-on's program crashes. The GM's health rows must name it as any other service, and the night's record must say the game ran this engine version with this add-on, or the night cannot be told truly afterwards.
For the designer. The pack already lists the abilities it requires. An add-on provides an ability. With add-ons, “this engine” means the release plus what is installed beside it.
For you. For ALN the difference is small, because you make the releases: an extension you want goes into the next release. The difference matters for everyone else.

For a production adopting the engine. A university with a developer writes support for its own lighting system. Under main-release-only they send it back and wait for a release, the path [[ex:EX21]] describes. Under add-ons they install it tonight and keep it across releases as long as the place it plugs into holds. Under their own build they run their own engine, and the community splits.

For the people maintaining the engine. Add-ons mean a second set of fixed places in the engine's code where outside code plugs in; they must stay stable across versions and be tested against code you did not write. Main-release-only means one body of code and one test run on two games. A production's own build costs you nothing and splits the platform's users.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “How games and venues extend the engine” asks where the engine leaves room for a developer to add a scoring model, a kind of screen, a device kind, a program it drives or a content source without touching the rest; whether those rooms are fixed places in the engine's code that outsiders install into, with their own versions, or places inside one body of code, is this question. “The published protocol's form”: whether a version names add-ons and whether add-on messages are allowed. “How one engine runs as many separate copies”: add-ons installed per copy.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on extensions. [[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]. [[qt:QT21]], [[qt:QT22]], [[qt:QT23]], [[ex:EX4]], [[ex:EX9]], [[ex:EX15]], [[ex:EX18]], [[ex:EX21]], [[ex:EX26]]. The roadmap's release block.

options.label: Main release only.
options.means: Every extension for all games comes back to the main line, through review and the developer's tests on two games, and reaches a production in a release. The version is one number, and your review decides what goes in.
options.cost: The simplest to keep and the slowest for adopters.

options.label: Add-ons installed beside the release, at named places.
options.means: A device kind, a program the engine drives, a scoring model, a kind of screen, a content source: the places the extension cases already name. Add-ons are loaded from the venue profile or a file of their own; the version mark and the night's record name them; the GM's health rows name them. Adopters move at their own pace.
options.cost: A fixed place in the engine's code for each kind of add-on, with its own version; a stand-in and tests per add-on; you keep those places stable and test releases against add-ons you did not write.

options.label: A production's own build, with no promise.
options.means: Nothing to build. This happens in any open-source project whatever you decide; the choice is only whether the engine helps (add-ons) or does not.
options.cost: Nothing to you. The production carries its own engine, its changes reach nobody else, and the platform's users split.

questions.recommendation: Ship the first release as main-release-only, and build the places where an add-on would plug in as fixed places in the engine's code with their own versions, so that add-ons can be allowed later without rebuilding; the places cost their versions and their tests from the first release; the version mark, the health rows and the night's record are designed to name an add-on from the start. What is promised to adopters about add-ons can wait for the release block, with the first adopters in view. From you now, because the panel's architect for growth and extension designs those places in the blind round: whether a production may ever run an extension the engine did not ship beside its engine, with the engine's help. A yes makes the places part of the published protocol's design; a no makes them one body of code, and the only path for an extension is the main release.

questions.title: Where the trial copy runs while a show runs
questions.decides: The designer's iteration speed against running well at the size of a show and testable without the live show. Whether a designer must be able to rehearse on a separate trial copy of the engine on the show machine while a show runs, or only between games on the show machine, or only on a laptop or the test bench. In other words, whether the show machine must carry two running copies of the engine during a show.
evidence: Settled by the requirements: no trial copy or test run ever touches the live show ([[qt:QT11]], settled by you; [[qt:QT27]], proposed). Open: whether a trial copy runs on the show machine during a show at all. The record disagrees with itself here. [[qt:QT11]] says you settled a trial copy on the same machine while a show runs, through the preview block and your ratification of the design tool's pages; [[ex:EX14]] and the decision ahead “How one engine runs as many separate copies” on [[page:design]] say where it runs is open; your ratification said the trial copy ships with its own profile, not where it runs; and the preview block names rehearsing on a running trial copy without saying where it runs.

At a show. The GM runs the show on the show machine. The designer at the desk starts a trial copy on the same machine to try tomorrow's pack. The trial's video player must not take the TV, its music must not come out of the room's speakers, and the machine's processor, and the heat it can shed, are shared with the live show. [[qt:QT11]] promises that the show never notices.
For the GM at a failure. A trial copy that misbehaves during a show is a risk the GM did not take. The strongest isolation the design can build is still weaker than a trial copy that is not there.

For the designer. On a laptop the designer rehearses on the test bench with stand-ins and never on the real room. Between games the designer rehearses on the real room and its equipment, but only before doors or after the last game. During a show the designer rehearses whenever they like.
For a production adopting the engine. A one-machine kit versus a kit with a laptop. A production with a small show machine and a long show.

For the people maintaining the engine. Two copies at once need separate files, ports, settings, programs and passes, and a share of the machine reserved for the show. One copy at a time needs separate files and records only.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “How one engine runs as many separate copies” says in what it decides that where the designer's trial copy runs is open. The answer decides how strong the isolation between copies must be and whether headroom is reserved on the show machine; it also feeds the limits under [[qt:QT33]] and the number of copies one machine must carry under [[qt:QT43]].
Sources. [[qt:QT11]], [[ex:EX14]], [[qt:QT27]], [[qt:QT43]], the decision ahead on copies on [[page:design]], and the roadmap's preview block.

options.label: During the show, on the same machine.
options.means: The designer rehearses whenever they like, on the real room's engine. The most convenient for the designer.
options.cost: The copies round must isolate at the level of the operating system and reserve headroom for the show; the most careful engineering to keep, for years.

options.label: Only between games, on the show machine.
options.means: Rehearsals on the real room happen before doors or after the last game.
options.cost: Separate files and records; no two copies scheduled together during a show.

options.label: Only on a laptop or the test bench.
options.means: The show machine runs one engine, ever. The real room is rehearsed only by running a game on it.
options.cost: The least to build; the designer never rehearses on the real equipment except by playing.

questions.recommendation: Whether the designer's convenience during a show is worth the risk to the show and the engineering to keep two copies apart on one small machine, or whether rehearsing between games and on a laptop is enough. The record's own sources say different things, so it cannot settle this for you.

groups.title: Standalone games
intro: Standalone games are a capability of the engine. From your words of 2026-11-02: games designed and set up to run where a network connection is not feasible, or where other logistics make it better to use only GM scanners, player scanners (phone or hardware), or both. A game declares it, and no game mixes networked and standalone devices ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]). Your words also answer the hardware scanner's standalone mode: it plays standalone games as the phone's scanner does. Where the declaration is held is for the design rounds. One reading of your words, that a standalone game may have no GM tablet at all, is listed under the readings to confirm below; the first question here asks the fuller version of it.

Two conflicts meet here. Every screen telling the truth against standalone and offline is settled: a standalone game says standalone, and every service the engine runs reads not installed tonight, grey. The standing rule of parity between phones and hardware scanners against standalone and offline is open in one part: whether a mechanic declared in the pack must run on a hardware scanner alone; that part belongs to the second question here and to “What a game's maker may build inside the pack” above.

questions.title: Which standalone games the engine must run
questions.decides: Which shapes of game with no show machine the engine must support, now and later. One GM tablet alone. Several GM tablets. Player scanners alone (phones, hardware scanners or both). GM and player scanners together. With no network at all between the devices, or with a small network (a phone's hotspot, the kit's router with no show machine). Whether one standalone game means one GM tablet. Whether “standalone” means no show machine, or means no network.
evidence: The decision entry holds one reading to confirm (a standalone game may have no GM tablet at all) and, in its history, the question “One GM tablet per standalone game?”; the record's open list now names this question in full, and no decision answers it ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]). The quality target [[qt:QT37]] and the extension case [[ex:EX12]] both name the shapes as your open question; [[qt:QT39]] asks whether a standalone game's record holds what the players found, which depends on the answer.

At a show. A game in a tent with battery power: one GM with a tablet, twenty players with phones. With the tablet alone, the GM sells and exposes tokens and the phones show memories, but nothing a player found reaches the GM's record; today's standalone game is this shape, and nothing records what players found. With two GM tablets and no network, today there are two games: a token can be sold at both tables, and the scores must be added by hand at the end ([[flaw:C1]]). With a hotspot and no show machine, the tablet could act as the engine for the phones; then the game is in truth a networked game with the tablet as the machine, and the question is whether you call that standalone. Your words name both reasons for a standalone game: a network that is not feasible, and logistics that make scanners alone preferable, which can hold in a room that has a network.
For the GM at a failure. With one tablet, the tablet is the only copy of the game. A broken tablet ends the record unless the game is copied somewhere as it runs.

For the designer. A pack for a standalone game must know what the devices can do alone. Two-tap actions between players' objects need one decider that both devices reach, so they need a network and a decider. A group bonus needs one claims list, so it needs one tablet or a merge rule. A designer who does not know the shapes designs mechanics that cannot run.

For a production adopting the engine. A school running a game on phones only, no GM. A museum running hardware scanners only, with a record collected at closing. A company with wifi but no spare computer, wanting the GM's tablet to be the machine. Each is a different product.

The cost grows down the list of shapes below. The first three need nothing shared between devices. The fourth is a second place the engine runs. The fifth is a merge of records. A link the agent notes, which you have not stated: if a networked game may carry on with its devices alone when the show machine fails (the question “The show machine fails mid-game”), several tablets with no engine is the same problem.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included” names the tablet in a standalone game as a decider; with several tablets or a tablet-as-engine the placement differs. “How the engine holds the game's state”: whether the record must live on a tablet, be copied between tablets, or be merged. “The published protocol's form”: whether devices ever speak to a tablet instead of the engine. “How one engine runs as many separate copies”: an engine on a tablet or a small computer is a copy on another kind of machine.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on standalone games. [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]. [[qt:QT37]], [[qt:QT39]], [[ex:EX12]]. The review of standalone games on [[page:today#standalone]]: two standalone tablets are two separate games; no channel joins the player devices to the tablet; nothing records what players found.

options.label: One GM tablet alone.
options.means: Today's shape. The tablet runs the game's rules; no channel between devices.
options.cost: The cheapest. Nothing a player found reaches the record.

options.label: Player scanners alone, content only.
options.means: Nothing shared. A record of what players found needs a collection step afterwards (each device exports; the design tool or a tablet merges), or there is no record.
options.cost: A collection step, or no record.

options.label: One GM tablet and player scanners, no network.
options.means: The two halves never meet; as the first two together. The GM's record holds no player finds.
options.cost: As the first two together.

options.label: One GM tablet as the engine for other devices over a small network.
options.means: An engine that runs where a tablet runs, or a small computer in the GM's bag. “Standalone” then means no show machine rather than no network. The later choice on the standalone tablet (the same parts the engine runs, or an engine of its own) becomes this shape's design.
options.cost: A second platform the engine must run on.

options.label: Several GM tablets with no network.
options.means: Either refused (one tablet per standalone game) or accepted as separate games merged afterwards under the conflict rule from “A GM tablet cut off from the engine”.
options.cost: A merge of records, or a refusal.

questions.recommendation: For each shape, whether it is required now, allowed later, or never; and whether “standalone” means no show machine or no network. Which productions and rooms the engine must serve is what the product is for, and the record cannot settle it.

questions.title: What a standalone game gives up, and what it keeps
questions.decides: Which of a pack's effects a game declared standalone may use, and what happens to the rest: evidence exposed in public (the scoreboard screen), video, the game clock with its phases, cues, music and lights, and the record of what players found. Whether the check at publish refuses a standalone game whose pack declares an effect no device can carry alone, or the game runs and shows each such effect as not installed tonight, or the designer marks each effect as skip-it or block-the-show. Whether a standalone game must leave a record of what players found.
evidence: What the screens draw for an exposed token or a video token with no engine is now the agent's call “[[call:exposed-evidence-and-video-with-no-engine]]”, listed below, and the record lists it there; [[qt:QT39]] marks open whether a standalone game's record holds what the players found at all. This question is the rule above that default.

At a show. In ALN a detective transaction exposes a token, which means its summary appears on the TV for everyone. With no TV the GM sees the summary once on the result screen and the public never does; “exposed means public” has no standalone effect today. A video token on the phone's scanner shows a black screen; on the hardware scanner it shows the picture and “video unavailable, rescan later”, which can never work ([[flaw:N1]]). The pack's game clock has no reader on a standalone tablet; the panel shows wall-clock time.

For the GM at a failure. Nothing fails; the point is that the GM should see at the start, grey and not red, “this game is standalone: video and public evidence are not available tonight”, the way [[qt:QT37]] asks.

For the designer. Under a strict rule the design tool refuses to publish a standalone game whose pack uses video or public evidence until the designer removes them or marks them skippable, the way [[ex:EX6]] lets a designer mark lights as skip-it or block-the-show. Under a lenient rule the pack publishes and the effects vanish quietly. The second game's pack already says the opposite thing, that the game needs an engine by nature ([[ex:EX20]]); a standalone declaration is the opposite of that statement.
For a production adopting the engine. A production built for phones only must know, before they design, which mechanics work with no machine. A rule that is written down is what they can design to.

And for the record of what players found: no record in a standalone game; a record from the GM tablet only (what teams turned in); or a record collected from every device afterwards. The last is the only one that makes a standalone night tellable the way a networked night is ([[promise:J3]]).

Which decision ahead depends on it. “How games and venues extend the engine”: what a pack may declare and how the check at publish refuses a pack that asks for something this engine lacks are in what it decides; a standalone declaration and the per-effect marks are pack format. “Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included”: what reads the declaration and on which device. “The published protocol's form”: the pack is one of its files, and the night's record (with or without player finds) is another.

Sources. Your comment of 2026-11-02 on standalone games. [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]. [[qt:QT6]], [[qt:QT37]], [[qt:QT39]], [[ex:EX6]], [[ex:EX12]], [[ex:EX20]], [[flaw:N1]]. The review of standalone games on [[page:today#standalone]].

options.label: Strict: the check at publish refuses a standalone game whose pack needs an engine-only effect, and names the effect.
options.means: The designer removes the effect or changes the declaration. No surprises at a show; some games cannot be standalone at all.
options.cost: The pack lists which effects need an engine (video, public screens, the clock, cues on equipment, hidden facts) and the check compares.

options.label: Grey and go: the game runs and every engine-only effect reads as not installed tonight.
options.means: Every standalone game is possible, by the same words the venue profile already uses for lights left at home. A designer learns what vanished only by playing.
options.cost: Each device must know the list and show it; nothing is refused.

options.label: Per-effect marks by the designer: skip-it or block-the-show, as lights carry today.
options.means: Block-the-show makes the game refuse to be standalone; skip-it lets it run grey. The most control.
options.cost: The most to write in the tool.

questions.recommendation: Per-effect marks by the designer, skip-it or block-the-show, with block-the-show refusing at publish and naming the effect. It is the pattern the pack already has for lights ([[ex:EX6]]), so adopters learn one rule, and it gives the designer the decision instead of the engine. For the record of what players found: a record from the GM tablet is the first step, and a record collected from every device afterwards is the goal, if you want standalone nights told the way networked nights are. From you: whether you do.

groups.title: Hardware
intro: Your decision: the hardware is fixed only in that ALN runs on the kit you bought; the mature engine is flexible about hardware, so the architecture must allow that flexibility later; and the current roadmap sets realistic bounds on how much is built now and where it names specific requirements ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]). The numbers that go with it (devices and phones per kit, set-up time, how long records are kept, a scanner's first sync) are not questions for you: the agent has sorted them into the engine's requirements, each production's settings and a few technical defaults, for you to review below ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]).

questions.title: Which hardware the first new engine requires, and what it must allow replacing
questions.decides: For each class of device in ALN's kit, whether it is a fixed requirement of the first release of the new engine (an adopter must bring the same) or a thing the engine's design must allow replacing later (a seam built now, no work beyond ALN's kit). The classes: the show machine (a Raspberry Pi 5 running Linux); the GM's station (an Android tablet running Chrome, reading NFC tokens itself); the players' devices (phones with a web page; one specific hardware scanner); the public screens (a TV over HDMI; the small computer that shows the scoreboard on a second screen); the room's programs (the video player, the music player, the sound system, Bluetooth speakers, the lighting system); and the kit's own network.
evidence: Much of this the requirements already settle. The engine must run a whole game on a laptop or a cloud machine with stand-ins ([[qt:QT25]]), so “a Linux computer” is already wider than “a Pi”. A different hardware scanner joins by its pass ([[qt:QT22]]). A different lighting system or video player changes only the code that talks to it ([[qt:QT23]], [[ex:EX15]]). The new extension case [[ex:EX28]] carries other hardware. What the requirements do not settle is the GM's station, and the readiness list for adopters.

For a production adopting the engine. A company whose GMs have iPads cannot run GM stations today: an iPad's browser cannot read NFC tokens, so the GM scanner cannot read them. A company with no hardware scanners, phones only, is fine. A company that wants the GM at a laptop with a separate token reader is not served. Adopters need to know what is a fixed requirement and what the engine allows ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]); the GM's station is the largest item on that list that nothing yet says.

At a show. If a GM station may be a laptop with a separate reader, then the device that reads a token and the device that decides may be two devices, which today they never are. And a laptop GM station could run the engine itself with a venue profile that names no equipment, which would make a standalone game “the engine on the GM's laptop” rather than “a tablet that copies the engine's rules”. That is a large simplification of the standalone questions, if you want it.

For the GM at a failure. A GM tablet dies mid-show. Today the spare must be another Android tablet with NFC, set up in advance. If the station may be any browser, the GM carries on from a laptop or a phone at hand, typing codes; that is one more fallback under [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]].

For the designer. The pack declares which kinds of device its players use and what part each plays (the standing rule “Equal in ability, not in screens”), so the list of device classes is part of the pack format and of the published protocol.
For the people maintaining the engine. Every class the engine must allow replacing needs a seam, a stand-in and a test. Every class fixed needs none of that now and all of it later, if ever.

What you must say now, and what the design rounds should propose. Now: whether the first release's fixed list is ALN's kit as it stands (the panel's setting states it as the first production's hardware, not as the engine's requirement); whether the GM's station must be allowed, in the architecture now, to be something other than an Android tablet reading NFC itself; and whether a tablet-class device or a GM's laptop must be able to run the engine itself, which joins the question “Which standalone games the engine must run”. The design rounds then propose the seams for the device kinds and the programs, which classes get stand-ins first, and the hardware the roadmap names as required at each of its stages, from the first show on the new engine to a release others can adopt, for you to decide.

Which decision ahead depends on it. “The published protocol's form”: the device kinds and passes it defines. “Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included”: whether a GM's device may run the engine itself changes what the standalone decider is. “How one engine runs as many separate copies”: an engine on a GM's laptop is a copy on another machine. The panel's setting, which lists ALN's devices as facts, changes if the GM station may be other devices, so this is needed before the blind round's folder is built.

Sources. Your comments of 2026-11-02 on hardware and on the numbers. [[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]] (“Where the current roadmap draws that line is open”). [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]. [[qt:QT22]], [[qt:QT23]], [[qt:QT25]], [[ex:EX27]], [[ex:EX28]], the standing rules on platform parity, [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]].

options.label: The GM's station: an Android tablet with built-in NFC, fixed.
options.means: Adopters buy the same tablets. The build is as today.
options.cost: The smallest set of GM devices to test, and a hard requirement in the adoption guide.

options.label: The GM's station: any browser, with the token reader as its own kind of device feeding it.
options.means: A GM at a laptop with a separate reader, or at an iPad with a camera reading printed codes. The GM's station is wherever the browser is, including a laptop that runs the engine.
options.cost: A reader device kind in the protocol; the GM app works with no NFC of its own; a station and a reader are paired.

options.label: The GM's station: any browser, with printed codes and typed codes when there is no NFC.
options.means: Slower GMs at venues without NFC devices, and no new device kind.
options.cost: Little for typed codes, since the GM app already has manual entry; reading printed codes with the camera is new to the GM app, though the phone's scanner already does it.

questions.recommendation: Whether the first release's fixed list is ALN's kit as it stands; whether the GM's station must be allowed, now, to be something other than an Android tablet reading NFC itself, and if so which of the three shapes above; and whether a GM's device must be able to run the engine. What the first release requires an adopter to buy, and whether your GMs' way of working is the engine's requirement or ALN's habit, is your business call.

groups.title: The panel
intro: You decided what the panel sees and when ([[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]) and said the context it gets is critical ([[dec:independent-architects-propose-the-top-level-design]]). Adding to what the blind round gets changes your decision, so that is your question. How the panel runs (its three lenses, and whether the second round reads today's code) is the agent's call, listed below with its reasons. Its brief is on [[page:design#panel]], revised on 2026-11-02 for your decisions of that day.

questions.title: What the panel gets in its blind round
questions.decides: Whether the panel's blind round also gets the decisions you have made that bind any design, and the six decisions ahead as its agenda, or only the goal, the requirements and the setting; and whether the agent's readings of your words that the record marks to be confirmed are kept from it, as the agent proposes. This question is yours because your decision on what the panel sees lists only the goal, the requirements and the setting, and adding to it changes that decision.
evidence: Your decision [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]] lists the goal, the requirements and the setting for the blind round, and names nothing else.

The decisions that bind any design: [[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]; [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]], with its purpose in your words; [[dec:four-words-for-the-game-s-live-facts]]; [[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]; [[dec:the-role-question-starts-from-settled-roles]]; and your four decisions of 2026-11-02: [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]], [[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]], [[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]] and [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]. They are your decisions, not the reasoning of the agent running the pass. Each goes to the panel in your own words from the decision record.

The agent proposes to withhold, either way, two of its readings of your words that the record marks to be confirmed and that the open questions do not already carry (that a tablet keeps taking scans while cut off; that a standalone game may have no GM tablet), and to give the panel the open questions instead, so it designs for both answers. The third reading, that the design must say how a networked game carries on if the show machine fails, reaches the panel as the question “The show machine fails mid-game” and in the state lens. The sorting of the quality targets' numbers reaches the panel through the requirements, marked there as the agent's call. Say so if you want the readings given.

The six decisions ahead are your list, from [[dec:design-top-down-hardest-to-reverse-choices-first]]. The last, how today's engine moves to the new design, waits for the second round, where today's engine is known.

The setting the blind round gets now presents ALN's kit as the first production's hardware, given as facts and not as the engine's requirements. If the GM's station may be other devices (the question “Which hardware the first new engine requires, and what it must allow replacing”), that sentence changes before the folder is built.
The panel runs only after you approve its brief and have reviewed the requirements. If anything else should be added to what the panel sees, or kept from it, say so with this question.

options.label: Also give the blind round your binding decisions and the six decisions ahead, with leave to add, split or merge decisions.
options.means: The architects design inside what you have already ruled, and spend their proposals on what is open.
options.cost: The agenda frames the architects' thinking; they are told they may change it if they say why.

options.label: Give the blind round only the goal, the requirements and the setting.
options.means: The architects start from nothing but the requirements.
options.cost: Proposals may break decisions you have already made, among them a game that pauses at a lost connection, and the synthesis must sort them out.

questions.recommendation: Also give the blind round your binding decisions and the six decisions ahead. A panel without them would spend its proposals on designs you have already ruled out, and it may still change the agenda if it says why.

readings.text: A standalone game may have no GM tablet at all: your words “gm and/or player scanners” read that way, so player scanners alone would be a shape the engine allows; the fuller question is “Which standalone games the engine must run” above.

A GM tablet that loses the engine keeps taking scans, and the game carries on, rather than refusing scans until the connection returns; your words point this way but did not name the choice, and it brings a cost: two tablets may sell the same token while apart, which must be sorted out afterwards (the question “A GM tablet cut off from the engine” above).

The design must say how a networked game carries on if the show machine itself fails; that meets your decision that no game mixes networked and standalone devices, and how the results come back together is the question “The show machine fails mid-game” above.

calls.title: Four readings of earlier decisions are confirmed
calls.call: Four earlier decisions are read as overtaken by later ones, as the decision record reads them: each build area no longer starts with its proof test failing on today's engine, unless the move from today's engine changes it in place ([[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]], [[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]]); the design rounds go by decision, not one design choice per question, the four questions on the game's live facts are no longer designed together as one rule, and the nine questions serve as checks on each design ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]], [[dec:five-documents-the-design-half-hands-over]], [[dec:when-the-design-half-is-finished]], [[dec:design-top-down-hardest-to-reverse-choices-first]]); the published protocol takes the place of the drafted message lists among the handover documents ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]); and the rig reproducing each finding marked for live proof is no longer a condition for ending the design half.
calls.why: Each reading follows from a later decision of yours that set the order of the work. Nothing a player, GM or designer meets changes; only how the pass runs. The earlier wordings stay in the record's history.

calls.title: The quality targets' numbers are sorted, not asked
calls.call: Each number a quality target needs is sorted as one of three kinds. An engine requirement or limit, which the engine states the same for every production and the tests measure (a tablet back under its name within five seconds; the minutes from publish to playing; how fast a scan is answered; how many scans each kind of device keeps while offline; how many copies one machine carries). A production's setting, which each production makes for itself with ALN's as the first set (power-on to a running show; set-up time; how long records are kept; the kit's devices and phones; a scanner's first sync). A technical default the agent proposes and a production may change (how the program watcher retries; how long before a screen says the engine is silent; the machine's load, memory, disk and temperature limits). The sorting is on each target on [[page:requirements]] and in the review below.
calls.why: You said many of these numbers are “stuff that the engine itself should be relatively agnostic about” ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]). A limit the engine is sized for is measured, not decided, and a production's numbers are that production's. The record marks the split itself as a reading of your words to be confirmed; the agent makes it as its call, which stands unless you overrule it. How the requirements are grouped is the agent's to propose and yours to overrule.

calls.title: The program watcher's retries
calls.call: Today the shared program watcher, which the music player uses, restarts a program four times, waiting ten seconds and doubling the wait each time (10, 20, 40, then 80 seconds), and shows red at the fifth failure; the video player's watcher waits a fixed three seconds, and the TV's browser has none. The agent starts from the shared watcher. The controls come back within ten seconds ([[qt:QT2]]).
calls.why: A technical default that serves every production the same way; it starts from today's code. Ten seconds is the engine's own behaviour, from the promise's test.

calls.title: How long before a screen says the engine is silent
calls.call: Ten seconds, which is how often both player scanners check on the engine today; the engine states the longest delay it allows ([[qt:QT5]]).
calls.why: The value trades network traffic against how fast a screen admits its numbers are old. That is a technical trade-off, and a production may change it.

calls.title: The show machine's limits
calls.call: The machine's load, memory, disk and temperature limits are proposed per supported machine, with ALN's Raspberry Pi 5 as the first ([[qt:QT33]]).
calls.why: The engine is meant to be flexible about hardware ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]), so no one machine's limits are the engine's.

calls.title: The missing standalone declaration is a design flaw of its own
calls.call: [[flaw:N1]] stays a design flaw of its own, holding the eight findings from the review of standalone games, rather than joining [[flaw:C9]], [[flaw:C11]] and [[flaw:C14]].
calls.why: Three other design choices (what each fact does between games, one answer per question, how old a copy is) need the declared fact as an input and would otherwise each invent their own answer. How findings are grouped is the agent's analysis.

calls.title: The tap promise is to be split in two
calls.call: [[promise:J3]] is to be split into “Every tap gets its answer” and “The night can be told afterwards” when the promises are next revised, after your review; until then [[page:requirements]] shows it as one promise, and the count of ten stands.
calls.why: The two halves serve different people at two moments, the GM or player at the tap and the director after the show, and share no part. How the requirements are worded and grouped is the agent's call ([[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]).

calls.title: The venue promise stays one
calls.call: One promise, titled “The game fits the venue it is in tonight” ([[promise:J8]]), with standalone games in its first sentences, and another production fitting the engine to its own venue and hardware named in its sentences.
calls.why: A separate promise for running in any setup would own no part. Your decision on what each production sets adds a person to its sentences, not a second promise.

calls.title: Proof and release stay one promise
calls.call: One promise, as the title of [[promise:J10]] has it. What release day means in practice moved to your question “Release day: what must update together, and how long older devices work”.
calls.why: Whether two moments sit in one promise or two is wording; every option gives the flaws the same parts to be fixed in. The product question inside release day is yours, and it is on this page.

calls.title: The route for equipment state is named in neither promise
calls.call: Neither [[promise:J4]] nor [[promise:J2]] names the route that carries the equipment's state to the screens, as long as the design rounds keep one delivery part; the card for [[flaw:C2]] stays under [[promise:J4]].
calls.why: This is where a sentence goes, so it is wording. The real choice behind it, one delivery part or several, belongs to the design rounds.

calls.title: Exposed evidence and video with no engine
calls.call: In a standalone game, the GM tablet gets a public evidence view of its own for exposed evidence, which it lacks today: its scoreboard screen is limited to ranking modes and the GM sees the summary once. A video token shows its picture with a plain note, never an error.
calls.why: A default for what a screen draws. Your words put standalone games in rooms where a network connection is not feasible, or where other logistics make it better to use only scanners, so the designer of such a game may have no TV; the engine's part is a default that works and never shows red. The rule above the default, which effects a standalone game may use, is your question “What a standalone game gives up, and what it keeps”.

calls.title: Every refused GM scan attempt is recorded
calls.call: The engine records every attempt and its answer, kept as long as the production keeps its records ([[qt:QT30]]), and shows it nowhere until a feature needs it.
calls.why: It changes nothing anyone sees. A fact not kept is lost for good, the after-game tools can read it later, and it helps sort out a game afterwards when a device failed mid-game ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]). You asked for the agent's view on this, and the view is the call.

calls.title: The panel's three lenses
calls.call: Three architects. The state lens becomes “state, authority and keeping the game going through a failure”, with [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]] as its first test. The growth lens names hardware flexibility and both kinds of extension. “Living with it” stays. No fourth architect.
calls.why: How the panel runs is the agent's call ([[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]). You called a paused game “the worst possible scenario”, so the state lens now names keeping the game going. Naming it in a lens costs nothing; a fourth architect costs two more agents and a longer synthesis.

calls.title: The second round reads today's code
calls.call: A fact sheet first, then the code and its component guides, to read only.
calls.why: Your decision gives the second round today's engine as facts and does not say in what form; the form is method. The code is the most exact fact about today's engine. It can pull a design toward small changes to today's engine, so the architects revise their own blind proposals rather than start again from the code.

review.title: The ten promises
review.what: What each person can count on at a given moment. Flag any that is missing, doubled or wrongly put; their wording is the agent's call, listed above. Two additions from version 9 stay in them for your review: the pack promise's two clauses (a second designer's game runs on the same engine; every device plays the same version of the pack and shows which) and the second half of the roles promise (only staff who log in start, pause, end or reset a game, run show control or change a score).

review.title: The quality targets
review.what: Forty-three targets under twelve qualities, each a situation that can be tested. Flag what is wrong or missing. Each number a target needs is sorted below as an engine requirement or limit, a production's setting (ALN's first) or a technical default; none waits on you as a decision.
numbers: [[qt:QT1]]: how long the engine may take from power back to a running show. A production's setting; the engine states its own restart time on each supported machine.

[[qt:QT2]]: how many restarts the program watcher tries, and over how long. A technical default (today the shared watcher, which the music player uses, restarts a program four times, waiting ten seconds and doubling the wait, and shows red at the fifth failure; the video player's waits a fixed three seconds, and the TV's browser has no watcher). Ten seconds for the controls to come back: an engine requirement.
[[qt:QT3]]: five seconds for a tablet to be back under its own station name. An engine requirement.
[[qt:QT5]]: how long after the engine goes silent a screen must say so. A technical default (today ten seconds); the engine states the longest delay it allows.
[[qt:QT9]]: the minutes from publish to playing. An engine requirement; a change moves only the small pack, and its media moves ahead of time, so the time does not grow with a production's media.
[[qt:QT13]]: how long the venue technician may need from an unpacked kit to a go. A production's setting.
[[qt:QT14]]: how long from power on to a running show. A production's setting; the engine states its own start time on each supported machine.
