[[qt:QT19]]: how long a newcomer may need to make and prove a first small change. An engine requirement.
[[qt:QT30]]: how long each kind of data is kept by default, per game. A production's setting; the engine ships a default.

[[qt:QT33]]: the kit size. A production's setting, ALN's being tonight's kit; the engine states the largest kit it supports, measured on each supported machine, and the agent proposes a few dozen devices, from ALN's show. The scan answer time, the message delivery time and half a second for a video to report started: engine requirements. The machine's load, memory, disk and temperature limits: technical defaults per supported machine.
[[qt:QT34]]: the number of player phones one kit carries. A production's setting, measured on its own machine and wifi.

[[qt:QT35]]: the longest acceptable first sync for a hardware scanner. A production's setting (ALN's first value is today's, 5 to 15 minutes for 30 to 40 MB); the engine states how fast each kind of scanner downloads.
[[qt:QT40]]: how many scans each kind of device must keep while offline. An engine limit stated per kind of device (today both player scanners keep 100).
[[qt:QT43]]: how many copies of the engine one machine must carry at once. An engine requirement; the situation already needs two.
[[qt:QT44]]: how long after a failure every GM tablet must show the fallbacks. An engine requirement.

review.title: The extension cases
review.what: Twenty-eight ways the platform must grow, each marked as one of your two kinds of extension or neither; your two examples are among them ([[ex:EX25]], [[ex:EX26]]), with another production adopting the engine ([[ex:EX27]]) and other hardware ([[ex:EX28]]). Flag any way of growing you plan that is missing, before the panel's brief is built.

review.title: The standing rules
review.what: The roadmap's standing constraints, one plain line each. They did not change on 2026-11-02, because the roadmap did not; flag any you no longer hold.

designRounds.text: How the engine holds the game's state: the facts of a running game that can change during it, where each is kept, how every screen's copy of them stays true, and how the game's state carries on through a failure and comes back together afterwards.

The published protocol's form: the protocol itself is decided; this round settles how each message and each file that crosses the engine's edge (what a device may ask, what the engine answers, what it tells screens, and the files that carry a game or a night) is defined and versioned, and the version rules your release-day answer sets.

Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included: which place decides each fact when a tablet is cut off, when the show machine fails, and when a game runs with no engine at all; and how what you choose under “A GM tablet cut off from the engine” is built.

How games and venues extend the engine: what a pack and a venue profile can declare, which of your two kinds of extension each change is, where a developer adds support for a device, a program, a scoring model or a content source, and where a production's own settings live.

How one engine runs as many separate copies: the show's copy, a trial copy and a test run on one machine, each keeping its own files, network ports and settings, a second kit on another machine, and a copy on different hardware. Where the designer's trial copy runs is your question “Where the trial copy runs while a show runs” above.

How today's engine moves to the new design: the build plan starts with a thin first version of the new design on the new test bench; whether today's engine is instead changed in place is part of this decision.

later.text: Where “this game is standalone” is declared: the venue profile (the earlier candidate favours it), the pack, the game's record or each device. It is decided in the round on where authority lives.
Getting facts onto screens: one delivery part for every fact, or the parts behind each promise delivering their own facts in one shared format.
The life of a game: one lifecycle part that alone moves the game and resets every part, or a table each part reads and applies itself.
The game rules as one shared body of code that the engine and the tablet both run, or two bodies kept equal by tests.
The equipment's interface: one per kind of thing the room can do (play a video, light a scene), or one per outside program.
The standalone tablet: the same record and lifecycle parts the engine runs, or an engine of its own.

How the fallback you choose under “The show machine fails mid-game” is built: how a networked game's state carries on without the show machine and comes back together afterwards, inside the rounds on how the engine holds the game's state and where authority lives; whatever is built must not make a mixed game by accident ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]).
The scoreboard: one page shown in two places, the TV's browser and the Pi 4, or a view inside the GM app.
The config tool, the designer's and venue technician's tool: a separate program that talks to the engine only by sending it requests, never by writing its files, or pages the engine itself serves.
When a changed pack may be loaded while the engine runs. That is not built yet; the requirements allow it only before a game starts or after it ends.

Where the setting lives that says whether the engine starts each outside program or uses one already running: in the venue technician's profile, as the earlier candidate has it, or in a file of its own, as the list of planned capabilities drawn from the roadmap has it. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

Where a production's own settings live (its kit's devices and phones, how long it keeps records): in the venue profile, in per-kit settings, or in both; and where the build plan places your answer to “Which hardware the first new engine requires, and what it must allow replacing” in the roadmap, as the hardware it names as a requirement and the hardware it leaves flexible. The first is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine; the second by the build plan ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]], [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]).

The order of the build half's work: by part (the earlier candidate put [[part:P13]] and [[part:P6]] first, since most flaws fall to them) or block by block, in the roadmap's order. The build plan, which starts with a thin first version, settles it after the design rounds.

Whether paper documents join the pack, with “unlocked” recorded during play, so the night's record can say which documents the players opened. “[[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]” left this to the design rounds; today the director marks them by hand after the show. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

How your answers to “How an extension for all games reaches a production” and “What a game's maker may build inside the pack” are built: the pack's format for what a maker declares, the places an add-on plugs into, and which piece each kind of extension changes in the design (the pack, the engine's code, an added outside service) ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]), in the round on how games and venues extend the engine, with the protocol's form.

entries.title: Design for the long term, beyond ALN
entries.line: The pass designs the best architecture for the engine's next iteration, for long-term use as it grows beyond ALN; the fixes and findings from the show machine in use now are clues to where today's design is off, never the driver.

entries.title: The architecture pass is the work now
entries.line: The pass is the current work, design half first, and covers the whole engine: the engine's server, the GM scanner, the two player scanners, the scoreboards and the config tool; today's engine keeps running the game on the show machine in use now until the new engine is ready to swap in on the new show machine, and no date governs the work.

entries.title: Blue's fixes are evidence of design causes
entries.line: The fixes made on the show machine in use now, and the findings left unfixed there, are evidence of where today's design is weak, never the driver; fixes that share a cause become one design decision, and the sixteen design flaws are test situations every design is checked against.

entries.title: Four words for the game's live facts
entries.line: Runtime state (every fact about a running game that can change during it), authority (the place that decides a fact), copy (that fact held anywhere else) and delivery path (its route from the authority to a screen) are in the glossary; an outside program can be an authority.

entries.title: Promises, qualities, moments, venue technician
entries.line: A promise is what a person can count on at a given moment; parts keep promises and design flaws break them; a quality is something every part must have so a promise holds everywhere; a moment is when a promise matters; the person who fits a kit to a venue is the venue technician; promises carry titles only.

entries.title: Name each step by what it does
entries.line: The pass has a design half and a build half; its steps are the requirements, the panel, the design rounds, the build plan, the hostile review, the final questions and your sign-off; blocks go by name, question rounds by date and test levels by name.

entries.title: The nine questions the pass answers
entries.line: The pass answers nine questions for the whole engine, from who decides each fact to whether a reconnecting screen's catch-up is built like its live update; the nine stand, and since the design went top-down they serve as checks on each design, a reading the agent confirms as its call, listed above.

entries.title: The role question starts from settled roles
entries.line: The components keep their settled roles: the player scanners show token content and report scans, with no scoring; the GM scanner is the command center; the scoreboards show the public results; the question on roles starts from these.

entries.title: Standalone games: declared, never mixed
entries.line: A game can be designed and set up to run with no engine, for a room where a network connection is not feasible or where other logistics make it better to use only GM scanners, player scanners (phone or hardware) or both; a game declares it, and no game mixes networked and standalone devices; standalone games join the list every design choice must serve. Your words of 2026-11-02 answer the hardware scanner's standalone mode: it plays standalone games as the phone's scanner does. Where the declaration is held is for the design rounds; which shapes the engine supports is your question above.

entries.title: The night's record and the after-game article
entries.line: What the players receive after the show is the game's business, outside the engine; the second half of the promise “[[promise:J3]]” names the director and the players after the show; the night's record carries the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw; players' emails stay outside the engine; the Director Console stays a separate program that reads the record; the two clocks (a sale stamped with the tablet's time, an adjustment with the engine computer's) join the flaw “[[flaw:C9]]”.

entries.title: One published protocol and an outside test bench
entries.line: One published, versioned protocol defines everything that crosses the engine's edge, the files that carry a game or a night included, and is designed in an early design round; the tests become a test bench outside the engine; proving each change before it reaches a show stays a quality every part must meet. Together they replace the earlier candidate's part “Joins and proofs”.

entries.title: No technical failure stops a game
entries.line: A lost connection or a device that goes down mid-game must not stop the game; at that moment the GMs must know the fallbacks that keep it running, with as little effect on the players as possible. Two readings follow, listed above for you to confirm: a cut-off tablet keeps taking scans and the game carries on; the design says how a networked game carries on if the show machine itself fails. The new quality target “[[qt:QT44]]” is the test.

entries.title: The engine is hardware-flexible; the roadmap sets the bounds
entries.line: The hardware is fixed only in that ALN runs on the kit you bought; the mature engine is flexible about hardware, so the fundamental architecture must allow that flexibility later; the current roadmap sets realistic bounds on how much of it is built now and where it names specific hardware requirements. Where the line falls is open, for the design rounds and the build plan; the part you must say now is your question above.

entries.title: Two kinds of game extension
entries.line: A mechanic built from what the engine can already do (a new action for the players, or a new way the game responds to a trigger the engine already has) should probably be the game's own maker's work, inside the game, perhaps shared with other makers later; your example is players changing the room's lighting by scanning tokens. A response the engine cannot give yet probably needs a developer's addition for every game; your example is a service for audio in several rooms. Your wording is tentative and the record keeps it so. What a maker may build inside the pack, and how an extension for all games reaches a production, are your questions above.

entries.title: The engine says what is fixed and what each production sets
entries.line: The engine stays agnostic about any one production's numbers (the devices and phones in a kit, power-on to a running show, set-up time, how long records are kept) and says which requirements are fixed and what each production sets for itself, so an adopter can fit it to their venue; ALN is the first production: one game, one venue, the hardware you bought. The sorting of the quality targets' numbers that follows is the agent's call, listed above.

decided.topic: How the design is made, and in what order

entries.title: One program: design half, then build half
entries.line: The design half decides the shared design choices with you, one question round at a time, and ends with the new roadmap; the build half changes the engine one area at a time, starting with a thin first version on a new test bench. That an area no longer starts with its test failing on today's engine is a reading the agent confirms as its call, listed above.

entries.title: Run the pass like the re-charter
entries.line: The pass is a roadmap revision run the way the September re-charter ran: evidence, a draft with questions, a hostile review, question rounds, your sign-off; its roadmap becomes the roadmap's next revision, and on your pages the questions go by title.

entries.title: The truth sweep's charter is retired
entries.line: The truth sweep's charter is retired; its purpose, proving that every screen tells the truth, moves into the build work the pass plans, and its survey of every screen and its five recorded bugs where a screen fell out of step with the engine are evidence for the pass.

entries.title: Five documents the design half hands over
entries.line: The design half hands over the design choices with proof tests in plain words, the review that named the design flaws with every fix and finding assigned or set aside, the published protocol in place of separate proposals for the message lists, one decision note per hard-to-reverse choice, and the new roadmap; the two parts read as overtaken are confirmed as the agent's call, listed above.

entries.title: The design half's method and tools
entries.line: The design half's order is the review that named the design flaws (done), the requirements, the panel, the design rounds, the build plan, the hostile review, the final questions and your sign-off; each round writes two or three designs side by side, published as pages for you and checked against the promises, the quality targets, the extension cases and the sixteen design flaws.

entries.title: When the design half is finished
entries.line: The design half ends at your sign-off once every finding and every fix made on the show machine in use now is assigned or set aside with a reason, every design choice says how it serves the planned capabilities and standalone games, and the hostile review's blocking findings are resolved; the two earlier conditions (one design choice per question, and the rig reproducing each finding marked for live proof) are read as overtaken, which the agent confirms as its call, listed above.

entries.title: Corrections to the readers and the hardening pieces
entries.line: The pieces of the hardening block already built (the kinds of equipment a pack can ask for and a venue profile can name, the code that marks equipment not installed tonight, and the smallest test set-up) stay in the engine, and the build half changes them only where a rule requires; the review's reading of today's code was split by source, merged by cause and checked, and that work is done.

entries.title: Build the test rig when building starts
entries.line: The test rig is built at the start of building, as part of the new test bench where a thin first version of the new design runs end to end, not before design; the exception is a move that changes today's engine in place. The question on how much the rig proves before design is withdrawn.

entries.title: Design top-down, hardest-to-reverse choices first
entries.line: The rest of the design half goes top-down: finish the requirements, then design rounds ordered by the hardest decisions to reverse (the six under “Coming in the design rounds”), each with two or three designs checked against the requirements and the sixteen design flaws, then a build plan that starts with a thin first version; this site is reframed to the long-term frame.

entries.title: Independent architects propose the top-level design
entries.line: An independent panel of architects, who have not seen the reasoning of the agent running the pass, proposes and stress-tests the top-level design decisions before the first design round; its brief comes to you first.

entries.title: What the architects' panel sees, and when
entries.line: In the blind round the panel gets the goal, the requirements and the setting; only after its first proposals does it get today's engine as facts and the sixteen design flaws as test situations; withheld are the recommendations of the agent running the pass, the earlier candidate (it enters the second round as one more proposal) and the earlier lists of design choices. It runs after you review the requirements. Whether it also gets your binding decisions and the decisions ahead is your question above.

entries.title: The owner's site: five linked pages
entries.line: Your site was five linked pages built from one set of data (the engine, decisions, promises, parts and design flaws), with earlier wordings and changes kept in a change log; nothing in the single page it replaced had to stay. The same decision asked for the long-term frame and titles in place of numbers, and version 9, published 2026-11-02, did both with six pages.

entries.title: The Decisions page holds only your decisions
entries.line: This page asks you only what you alone can decide, each question explained by what it means in practice; choices that are the agent's to make (how the requirements are worded and grouped, how the panel runs, technical defaults, and readings that follow from your earlier decisions) are listed as the agent's calls with their reasons, for you to overrule; the requirements are offered for review, not as decisions.

entries.title: Green's follow-ups ship when the definition session ends
entries.line: The new show machine's three follow-ups (a false boot warning on a correctly built new machine, two lines missing from the settings template, an install instruction the new operating system refuses) shipped as one small task when the definition session ended, on 2026-10-30.

entries.title: Decide in question rounds, never at sign-off
entries.line: Every decision is made in a question round with the evidence in view and written into its document at once; documents record decisions and never make them; anything new found while writing comes back to you as a question; your sign-off is a skim with no new decisions.

entries.title: The owner ratified the program document
entries.line: You ratified the program document, the plan for the architecture pass, on 2026-10-30; the definition session closed and the pass became the current work, design half first.

entries.title: No rule for documents: fix as we go
entries.line: The pass has no rule for written documents (guides, READMEs, contracts, code comments) that disagree with the code; they are fixed as we go, by the same piece of work that finds the disagreement; dated records stay as written.

entries.title: Titles, not numbers, and a topic record
entries.line: Decisions, questions and design flaws go by short plain titles in conversation and on your pages, ids stay inside records, and the decision record is reorganized by topic, each decision written as current truth with a dated history beneath.
